neutral_facts.value: The accused persons attacked the deceased and complainant party with lathis, farsa, and handmade bombs. The prosecution presented evidence showing the accused were part of an unlawful assembly with a common object to assault the deceased, who succumbed to the injuries inflicted. Witnesses, including those related to the deceased, testified about the incident and sustained injuries. The trial court acquitted the accused, but the High Court reversed this decision, finding the prosecution's version credible and the accused as aggressors. The accused were armed with lethal weapons and hurled abuses at the deceased, with one of them throwing a bomb on the deceased's chest, leading to his death.

quotes.text: The investigating agency in the course of investigation prepared the spot map, collected the bloodstained soil from the place of incident, and further, as is demonstrable, on being led by the accused persons seized the weapons, namely, lathi, farsa and handmade bombs and, thereafter, sent the seized articles to the chemical examiner for analysis.

Being dissatisfied with the judgment of acquittal, the State preferred the criminal appeal against the six accused persons. During the pendency of the appeal Mangal Singh expired and the appeal stood abated against him. The High court reappreciated the evidence on record and opined that the view expressed by the learned trial Judge was totally incorrect and could not be regarded as a plausible one and, accordingly, reversed the same and recorded the conviction and imposed the sentence as has been stated hereinbefore.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the accused persons formed an unlawful assembly with a common object to assault the deceased, who succumbed to the injuries inflicted. The prosecution established the presence and active participation of the appellant as a member of the unlawful assembly, and that the accused were the aggressors who hurled abuses and threw bombs at the deceased.

quotes.text: The prosecution was able to establish not only the appellant's presence but also his active participation as a member of the unlawful assembly. He might not have thrown the bomb at the deceased, but thereby he would not cease to be a member of the unlawful assembly as understood within the ambit of Section 149 IPC and there is ample evidence on record to safely conclude that all the accused persons who have been convicted by the High Court had formed an unlawful assembly and there was common object to assault the deceased who succumbed to the injuries inflicted on him.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the trial court's acquittal was plausible and that the High Court should not have reversed it. They contended that the prosecution failed to explain why other witnesses were not examined and that the appellant should not be convicted under Section 302 IPC as he did not directly assault the deceased.

quotes.text: It is submitted by Mr. Sharma, learned counsel for the appellant that the High Court while unsettling an order of acquittal should exercise the appellate power with great care and caution and it must be for substantial compelling reasons and the appellate court should not reverse a judgment of acquittal unless it finds that the same is totally perverse and wholly unsustainable.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the punishment under Section 149 IPC is vicarious and does not require each member of the unlawful assembly to commit an overt act. The court emphasized that mere presence in an unlawful assembly can make one liable if the common object of the assembly is to commit an offence.

quotes.text: The punishment prescribed by Section 149 is in a sense vicarious and does not always proceed on the basis that the offence has been actually committed by every member of the unlawful assembly.
